title: Ultrafast order-selective electron imaging and spectroscopy
authors: Jan Philipp Bange, Till Domröse, Claus Ropers, Stefan Mathias, Marcel Reutzel, .
abstract: Ultrafast pump-probe spectroscopies in energy and momentum have become indispensable for probing non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum materials, revealing pathways in ultrafast energy conversion and light-induced phase transitions. Different modalities uniquely access the coupled lattice, charge, and spin degrees of freedom that underpin the functionality of these materials. However, investigating technologically relevant nanoscale devices also requires high spatial resolution. Although electron microscopy provides nanometer-scale imaging, it frequently lacks the simultaneous ultrafast temporal resolution and spectroscopic specificity needed for such studies. In this perspective, we review recent advances in dark-field electron and photoelectron microscopy, focusing on two complementary techniques: femtosecond photoelectron momentum microscopy and ultrafast transmission electron microscopy. Their application enables comprehensive insights into the ultrafast dynamics of the electron, lattice, and spin subsystems. These order-selective electron imaging and spectroscopy techniques open broad scientific opportunities for a microscopic understanding of non-equilibrium phenomena in quantum materials, nanostructures and devices.
summary: This perspective reviews cutting-edge electron microscopy techniques designed to image ultrafast dynamics in quantum materials. By combining femtosecond time resolution with momentum-selective dark-field imaging, researchers can now microscopically track coupled electronic, lattice, and spin dynamics. This advancement opens new avenues for understanding non-equilibrium phenomena in nanoscale quantum devices.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing techniques to simultaneously achieve high spatial resolution, ultrafast temporal resolution, and spectroscopic specificity (energy and momentum) to probe non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum materials.
main_result: The review highlights that combining ultrafast dark-field electron microscopy (like femtosecond photoelectron momentum microscopy and UTEM) allows for momentum-selective nano-imaging of femtosecond dynamics, providing comprehensive insights into coupled electronic and structural subsystems.
method: The paper reviews advanced dark-field electron and photoelectron microscopy techniques, specifically femtosecond photoelectron momentum microscopy and ultrafast transmission electron microscopy.
model_or_system: The research focuses on technologically relevant quantum materials, nanostructures, and devices, including 2D heterostructures (e.g., WSe2/MoS2) and charge-density wave (CDW) systems (e.g., 1T-TaS2).
key_observables: Electronic band structure, quasiparticle dispersion relations, structural order parameters (e.g., CDW amplitude), and ultrafast carrier dynamics.
important_parameters: Femtosecond timescales, nanometer spatial resolution, and momentum-resolved observables (k-space).
main_assumptions: The primary limitation addressed is that traditional techniques often average over macroscopic areas or lack momentum resolution, necessitating the development of dark-field filtering approaches.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the need for simultaneous nanometer spatial, ultrafast temporal, and spectroscopic sensitivity. Figure 2 details the concepts of dark-field filtering for momentum selection in both photoelectron microscopy and UTEM.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a review, first establishing the scientific need (Sec. I), then reviewing the general concepts of dark-field electron microscopy (Sec. II), detailing specific implementations in momentum microscopy (Sec. III), and finally presenting applications and outlook in UTEM (Sec. IV).
why_interesting: The techniques discussed—especially momentum-resolved, time-dependent imaging—are crucial for mapping out the complex energy landscapes and phase transitions in strongly correlated electron systems, which is a major area of theoretical interest.
